subtitle: Midterm Important Subjective Questions (Solved)
topics: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: On what principle should progressivism focus? (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Ideas should be tested by active experimentation. Learning is rooted in the questions of learners in interaction with others. It is experience-based and student-centered.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Explain postmodernism in your own words.
subjective.answer: Postmodernism means literally 'after the modern era'. The modern era was the time of certainty and stretched from the 18th century to the late 20th century. Postmodernists believe that this era was far more predictable than the times we live in today; e.g., jobs were for life and class was a major source of identity. Since around the 1970s we have been living in times characterized by risk and diversity, and this has had huge implications for education. Postmodernism is a continuation of the modernist view; it does not mourn the loss of history, self, religion and center. It is a term applied to all human sciences — anthropology, psychology, architecture, history, etc. It is a reaction to modernism: systematic skepticism, and it is anti-foundational.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Who are the proponents of essentialism?
subjective.answer: The key proponents of essentialism are: William Bagley, Arthur Bestor, E. D. Hirsch, Chester Finn, Diane Ravitch and Theodore Sizer.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Differentiate between the curriculum of idealism and realism. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Realism curriculum: The curriculum consists of the basics — math, science, reading, etc. Attention is given to didactic and object studies in education (use of pictures, TV and videos in the educational process). Use of objects in education (Montessori). Emphasis is on subject matter, which is highly organized and systematic in approach. Idealism curriculum: Examining the roots of contemporary problems in the past (great literature/classics, etc.). Education at any level should teach students to think. It follows a subject-matter curriculum and a back-to-basics approach in education.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Write the application of education using epistemology and metaphysics under progressivism and pragmatism. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Metaphysics — What is real? Does it have meaning? Reality is in flux and ever-changing, so meaning is in the context of the individual, who is a "problem-solver." Epistemology — Knowledge and knowing: What is truth? Knowledge is gained via individual experience. Truth is individually defined, so the emphasis is on learning how to learn. Axiology — Values, ethics and aesthetics are determined by each individual in interaction with his/her culture, based on the shared values of the community or culture. Logic — Emphasis is on inductive thinking and problem solving. The teacher's role: The teacher is a facilitator of student learning; he/she provides resources for students' problem-solving abilities, develops students' problem-solving abilities and helps students to do what they want to do. The student: Learns by doing and discovering.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Write the application of education using epistemology and metaphysics under essentialism and realism. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: Metaphysics — What is real? Does it have meaning? What is relevant is what helps an individual live well and what benefits humanity. Epistemology — Knowledge and knowing: What is truth? Truth exists in the classics and modern science. Students must learn process and content. Knowledge is gained through the interaction of experiences and rational thought. Axiology — Values, ethics and aesthetics are determined by the natural order of things; values exist in the best of culture. Logic — How do we think? Deductive and inductive. Rationality is best developed through the interplay of deductive and inductive thinking.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Under realism and essentialism, what are the roles of the teacher and the student?
subjective.answer: Role of the teacher: The teacher has a social grounding in science, math and the humanities; relies on test scores to place students (competency testing of students with various methods); readily adopts new technology; enables students to learn objective methods of evaluating works; the teacher's responsibility is to teach skills and disciplined knowledge; the teacher should be competent in a specific subject matter, presenting ideas in a clear and consistent manner and demonstrating that there are definite ways to judge works of art, music, poetry and literature. The student: Is there to listen and learn.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: What is the role of the teacher and the student under idealism and perennialism?
subjective.answer: Role of the teacher: The teacher is an expert of content knowledge and passes on to the next generation the accumulated wisdom of the past. The student: Is there to learn what is taught.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Write about the role of teachers and students under pragmatism and progressivism.
subjective.answer: The teacher's role: The teacher is a facilitator of student learning; he/she provides resources for students' problem-solving abilities, develops students' problem-solving abilities, and helps students to do what they want to do. The student: Learns by doing and discovering.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Define eclecticism.
subjective.answer: There is a way of dealing with all the various models. Eclecticism is not a philosophical system or model, but rather the synthesizing and personal interpretation of various models to draw out the best components for you. Thus, you pull the best from various models in an effort to build your own statement of personal philosophy.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: What is existentialism and who are its key proponents?
subjective.answer: Existentialism: Reality is subjective, within the individual — the individual rather than external standards. Its key proponents are Sartre and Kierkegaard.

subjective.topic: Philosophical Foundations and Philosophies of Education
subjective.question: Define phenomenology theory in your own words.
subjective.answer: Phenomenology examines patterns of subjective experience and consciousness. It focuses upon a systematic reflection on, and investigation of, the structures of consciousness: realist concepts can be examined scientifically. It is based solely on consciousness. Individuals will be influenced by others, but do not have the same experience. It views the social world as a multiform structure of inner subjectivity and group understanding/unity. For example, a hammer is many things to many people: to a carpenter it is a tool; to a retailer it is merchandise; to a lecturer it is a prop.

subjective.question: Define psychology. (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Psychology is the scientific study of mental functions and behaviors, including: perception, cognition, behavior, emotion, personality and interpersonal relationships.

subjective.question: On what principle should the cognitivist focus? (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: The cognitivist focuses on how individuals process information. There is emphasis on memory (storage, retrieval and types); chunking can aid working memory, which is limited. Successful learners transfer information to long-term memory, which is "infinite" in capacity.

subjective.question: Write down the characteristics of cognitive psychology.
subjective.answer: The characteristics of cognitive psychology are: it focuses on how individuals process information; it emphasizes memory (storage, retrieval and types) — chunking can aid working memory, which is limited; and successful learners transfer information to long-term memory, which is "infinite" in capacity. Cognitive psychology replaced behaviorism as the dominant philosophy in the 1960s, because behaviorism did not explain language and learning, why people respond differently to the same stimulus, and that reinforcement can reduce motivation.

subjective.question: What is meant by the theory of behaviorism?
subjective.answer: Behaviorism focuses on stimulus-response and reinforcers. It studies conditioning — modifying or shaping behavior through reinforcement and rewards.

subjective.question: Explain Thorndike's law of exercise.
subjective.answer: Law of Exercise: The strength of connections is proportional to the frequency, duration and intensity of its occurrence. It justifies drill, repetition and review, and is seen today in behavior modification and basic skill instruction.

subjective.question: Describe the law of readiness.
subjective.answer: Law of Readiness: It is often misinterpreted as educational readiness. It deals with attitudes and focuses on "Why should I do this?" If the nervous system is ready, conduction is satisfying, and lack of conduction is annoying.

subjective.question: What was James Watson's contribution to Pavlov's theory?
subjective.answer: Watson took Pavlov's findings to another level. He emphasized that learning was observable or measurable, not cognitive. He believed the key to learning was in conditioning a child from an early age based on Pavlov's methods. His work raised the nurture versus nature question: Watson's theories strengthened the argument for the influence of experiences as opposed to genetics.

subjective.question: Identify the type of conditioning in the following example and explain why it applies: "Your father gives you a credit card at the end of your first year in college because you did so well. As a result, your grades continue to get better in your second year."
subjective.answer: Operant conditioning is used. In operant conditioning, secondary reinforcers are personally important, such as approval of friends or teachers, winning money, awards or recognition. Secondary reinforcers can become primary. Due to the wide range of secondary reinforcers, Skinner referred to them as generalized. The credit card is a secondary (generalized) reinforcer: receiving it after good performance strengthened the student's studying behavior, so his grades continued to improve.

subjective.question: Explain operant conditioning with examples from daily life.
subjective.answer: Operant conditioning is a type of learning in which behavior is controlled by consequences. Its key concepts are positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, positive punishment and negative punishment. Positive reinforcement is giving something pleasant after a behavior; this increases the probability that the behavior will continue. Examples: having a job and going to work every day to receive a paycheck; receiving praise after a musical performance increases the amount that you perform; a teacher complimenting students when they answer correctly increases that behavior; in the Skinner Box experiment, a rat got food as a reward for acceptable behavior, such as pressing a lever. Negative reinforcement is taking away something unpleasant as a result of acceptable behavior; this is also meant to increase the behavior. Examples: it is very noisy outside, so you turn on the television to mask the noise; a teacher exempts a student from the final test if he/she has perfect attendance — the teacher takes away something unpleasant to increase the behavior.

subjective.question: Give examples of positive punishment and negative punishment from your daily life. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Positive punishment means presenting an unpleasant consequence after an unwanted behavior in order to suppress it. Example: a teacher addresses the students in a firm tone and announces that they will have to pay a fine if they score lower than 75% in tomorrow's test. Negative punishment means removing something pleasant after an unwanted behavior (response cost). Example: a student who does not keep up his/her grades loses the label of class monitor or "student of the week" that he/she had earned earlier.

subjective.question: Give examples of reward and punishment in our daily life.
subjective.answer: Reward: A student works hard to get an A grade and faces a lot of hardships in the process, but when he succeeds, the appreciation or reward he gets from his teachers, parents and fellows convinces him that he chose the right path; he works harder in the future to repeat the process and maintain his position. Similarly, if a student completes his assignment on time or gets good marks in a class test, he may be awarded a label, i.e. "student of the week", or a reward, i.e. a new geometry box, in return. It is the duty of the teacher to improve optimistic behavior with positive reinforcement. Punishment: Addressing students in a firm tone to prepare enthusiastically for tomorrow's test, or they will have to pay a fine if they get lower marks than 75%. A response cost may also have to be paid, like taking back the label of class monitor or student of the week/month/year if they do not keep up their grades.

subjective.question: Define scaffolding. (Marks: 2)
subjective.answer: Scaffolding is the "role of teachers and others in supporting the learner's development and providing support structures to get to the next stage or level." In an educational context, scaffolding is an instructional structure whereby the teacher models the desired learning strategy or task, then gradually shifts responsibility to the students. Scaffolding provides support, extends the range of what a learner can do, allows the learner to accomplish tasks otherwise impossible, and is used only when needed.

subjective.question: Give an example of scaffolding in a classroom setting.
subjective.answer: In a classroom, a teacher who wants students to learn how to solve a new type of mathematics problem first solves one problem herself on the board, thinking aloud and showing each step (modelling). She then solves the next problem together with the class, asking students to suggest each step. Finally, she gives similar problems for students to solve independently and withdraws her help. In this way the teacher's support structure enables learners to accomplish a task they could not do alone, and the responsibility gradually shifts from the teacher to the students.

subjective.question: How does Robert Gagne define the theory of learning? (Marks: 3)
subjective.answer: Based upon his analysis of research, Gagne believed that the set of variables influencing the learning of tasks in one domain may not influence the learning of tasks in other domains. One may generalize research findings to other tasks within that domain, but not to tasks in other domains. Thus, factors found to influence the learning of one piece of information (e.g., overlearning positively affects the learning of telephone numbers) may be applied to other tasks in that domain (e.g., the learning of names), but not to tasks in other domains (e.g., the learning of a new concept). Gagne stressed the cumulative nature of learning intellectual skills, in which mastery of higher-level skills depends on the mastery of the simpler skills below them.

subjective.question: Write the important points of Robert Gagne's hierarchy of learning.
subjective.answer: Gagne's hierarchy of learning has eight levels, from simple to complex: 1. Signal learning (behavioral): Classical conditioning — response to a signal; learning by association. 2. Stimulus-response (behavioral): Operant conditioning — response to a given stimulus; learning through reinforcement. 3. Motor chains (behavioral): Linking two or more stimulus-response connections to form a more complex skill. 4. Verbal association (behavioral): Linking two or more words or ideas. 5. Multiple discriminations (behavioral): Responding in different ways to different items in a set. 6. Concept learning (behavioral–cognitive): Reacting to stimuli in an abstract way. 7. Rule learning (behavioral–cognitive): Chaining two or more stimulus situations or concepts. 8. Problem solving (cognitive): Combining known rules/principles into new situations to solve a problem.

subjective.question: How can we apply Gagne's theory in our classroom?
subjective.answer: Under Gagne's theory, teachers need to observe and relate lessons to students' interests so that it is easier for the students to understand. Teachers then need to gain attention, and this can be done by showing PowerPoints, diagrams and videos, etc., to help inform the students of what they will be learning. The teacher will then present the stimulus, for example by demonstrating how to perform the task (such as how to create a diagram). The teacher will be there for guidance and will then assess the performance of the students. The students will be active listeners and will learn how to perform various tasks; the student will have established an interest and will use prior knowledge to perform a new task. The students will complete the task and then give feedback as to what they have learned. They will then be able to apply their newly acquired skills in their everyday lives on their own, so that they actually have a learning experience.

subjective.question: Explain the pre-operational stage of Piaget's cognitive development with an example.
subjective.answer: The preoperational stage lasts from 2 to 7 years. The child can speak and print words. His memory and imagination develop. His thinking is often not logical, and much egocentric thinking occurs. He learns that symbols represent something else. Examples of acquisitions: Language — rapid expansion of vocabulary and grammatical structures; Extensive pretend play — enactment of true-to-life or fanciful scenarios with plots and assigned roles (e.g., mommy, doctor, Superman); Intuitive thought — some logical thinking based on "hunches" and "intuition" rather than on conscious awareness of logical principles (especially after age 4). For example, a child in this stage uses a stick as a horse in pretend play, because he can now let one thing symbolically represent another.

subjective.question: Explain the concrete operational stage of cognitive development by Piaget and also give examples. (Marks: 5)
subjective.answer: The concrete operational stage lasts from 7 to 11 years. The child has the ability to do simple math and measurement, with manipulatives. He begins to understand cause and effect. He can think about real, concrete things in systematic ways, but cannot understand abstract concepts. He is no longer egocentric; he can now understand other people's points of view. Examples of acquisitions: Distinction between one's own and others' perspectives — recognition that one's own thoughts and feelings may be different from those of others and do not necessarily reflect reality; Class inclusion — ability to classify objects as belonging to two or more categories simultaneously; Conservation — realization that amount stays the same if nothing is added or taken away, regardless of alterations in shape or arrangement (for example, a short glass of water holds the same amount as a tall glass half full of water); Reversibility — an action can be undone or reverted to its previous state (a ball of clay can be made into a clay bowl, but it can be reformed into a ball of clay).

subjective.question: What was Maria Montessori's contribution to education?
subjective.answer: What she did: At the Psychiatric Clinic at the University of Rome, she taught "difficult" children to read at a normal level. In 1906 she was asked to start a progressive school for the slum children of Italy — Casa dei Bambini (Children's House). Why she was important: She was a pioneer of child advocacy — for exceptional children and low-SES children. (The Tyler and Taba traditional vs. progressive study is also discussed in connection with her work; a modern irony is the expense of Montessori schools.)
